THOUGHT: Young patient in a high-speed deceleration MVC with hypotension, tachycardia, severe hypoxia and altered mental status — overall picture of traumatic shock/respiratory failure. Chest X‑ray shows widened mediastinum (classic for traumatic aortic injury), deviation of the nasogastric tube and mediastinal structures to the right (mass effect from a left‑sided mediastinal/pleural collection), fractured left second rib, and depression/compression of the left mainstem bronchus. On exam there are decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion at the left base — findings most consistent with a large left hemothorax rather than pneumothorax (which would be hyperresonant). Hemoglobin is preserved acutely, as expected early after hemorrhage. Taken together in the setting of high‑speed deceleration, the most likely unifying diagnosis is traumatic thoracic aortic injury (classically at the isthmus) with resultant mediastinal hemorrhage and a massive left hemothorax causing respiratory compromise and shock.

DIAGNOSIS: Traumatic thoracic aortic injury (aortic isthmus transection) with massive left-sided hemothorax.
